facts.claim: Anthropic (October 20, 2025): constantly clicking “approve” can lead to approval fatigue, where people stop paying close attention to what they approve.
Anthropic reported in October 2025 that, in its own internal use, sandboxing Claude Code safely cut permission prompts by 84% (vendor-reported).
Simon Willison (April 2023): gating an assistant’s actions on human approval won’t work well, because people learn to click OK to everything as fast as possible.
OWASP’s Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025: an indirect prompt injection reaches the model through input from outside sources, such as websites or files.
Simon Willison (June 2025): language models happily follow any instructions that reach them, whether or not they came from their operator.
Willison’s lethal trifecta (June 2025): private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate outside. The only safe course is never to combine all three.
Stripe’s card spending controls limit the total spent over an interval of time, such as a day or a month, not only each payment on its own.
Claude Code’s permissions docs: a “don’t ask again” yes for editing files lasts until the session ends; one for a shell command lasts permanently, per repository and command.
OWASP’s mitigations for prompt injection include human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations, and clearly marking untrusted outside content.
Willison’s dual-model pattern (April 2023): a privileged model takes input only from trusted sources and acts; a quarantined model reads untrusted content and has no tools.
Debenedetti et al. (CaMeL, 2025) take the steps of a task from the trusted request alone, so untrusted data the model reads can never change what the program does.
In the CaMeL paper (2025), the design solved 77% of AgentDojo’s tasks with provable security, against 84% for the same system with no defence.
